idiom_name: goroutine-local ownership plus channel hand-off (sync.Pool per-P shards, runtime.LockOSThread for affinity)
implementation_notes: Go deliberately has no thread-local storage and multiplexes goroutines over OS threads, so 'confine the object to one thread' becomes 'confine it to one goroutine' - or better, keep it as ordinary local state: a goroutine's variables are private to it and need no synchronization, and the race detector plus the culture of passing ownership make escapes visible. Where data must move, the idiom is a channel transfer: only one goroutine holds the value at a time ('share memory by communicating'), which replaces the classic shared structure with message passing. For genuinely thread-affine state (cgo libraries, OpenGL/GLib contexts, kernel state changed per OS thread) `runtime.LockOSThread` pins the goroutine to its thread; `sync.Pool` is the runtime's own confinement trick - a per-P private slot plus shared queue - for scratch objects whose fast path takes no locks.
pitfalls: LockOSThread without a matching UnlockOSThread permanently ties the goroutine to its thread and lets the runtime exit the thread with it - a silent resource leak.
A channel transfers a reference only by convention: keeping and mutating the sent pointer on the sender side is a data race the compiler accepts (the race detector only finds it when exercised).
sync.Pool is a cache, not a guarantee: items may be dropped at any GC, Get may return a fresh object, and pooled objects must never be assumed to hold prior state or capacity.
